quote: do have and recover of and from the defendant the net sum of $29,100,000

quote: the treaty process was “a fraud from beginning to end, manipulated, directed, and controlled by Indian agents and superintendents
summary: TREC's four-part fraud theory: (1) signatures chosen by US, bypassing Council of 44; (2) oral agreements omitted; technical boundary language not understood; (3) pre-written, arbitrary annuity amounts not yet appropriated (none appropriated for 1867-68 treaties as of March 3, 1869); (4) treaties are contracts of adhesion that courts should construe for the weaker party.

citation: Testimony in relation to the Ute Indian Outbreak (1880); ARCIA 1879 Meeker telegram Sept. 10, 1879; H.R. Misc. Doc. 38, 46th Cong., 2d Sess., p. 158 and testimony of Charles Adams
quote: at the crossing of Milk Creek, right at the line of the reservation as we then understood it
summary: Meeker's plowing of contested pasture and his Sept. 10 telegram reporting assault by Johnson (Canalla) are confirmed. The battle was at the Milk Creek crossing on the reservation line, and Adams testified the Utes saw Thornburgh's advance as bad faith after he first agreed to meet halfway. That Meeker's assault claim was false is not established by these sources.

quote: Otto Mears... began to bribe the Ute men for their signatures at two dollars apiece.
summary: Ratification required signatures of three-fourths of Ute adult men. Most Uncompahgre and Southern Utes refused; Ouray died in Aug 1880 without signing the ratification (per Conetah). Commissioner Otto Mears then paid Ute men two dollars per signature. Chairman Manypenny refused to approve and Mears was ordered to Washington, but Secretary Kirkwood dropped charges and reimbursed Mears for the bribes.

citation: ARCIA 1881, Report of the Ute Commission, Jan. 20, 1881 (signed Manypenny, Meacham, Bowman, Russell, Mears); ARCIA 1881, Report of Ute Commission pp.201-207; 21 Stat. 199-200 (three-fourths proviso)
quote: It was found that the names obtained at both agencies aggregated 581 adult male Ute Indians of the confederated bands in Colorado.
summary: The 1880 Act required signatures of three-fourths of adult males. The Ute Commission reported 581 adult male signatures by Sept. 25, 1880, which it judged over three-fourths, and noted Ouray's death and Kaniache's death by lightning. Its report, signed by chairman Manypenny and by Mears, says signers acted "without restraint and of their own accord", and records that Southern Ute signers expected "the money promised them" (the $60,000 per capita distribution provided in the agreement). The $2 per signature payments by Mears, Manypenny's refusal to approve, and Kirkwood's reimbursement come from Conetah (1982) via PSL and are not supported by this record; Manypenny signed the report that treated ratification as complete.

citation: ARCIA 1887, Commissioner's report on the Colorow affair; ARCIA 1887 p. LXXIX-LXXXII
quote: The Indian loss in this fight is said to be one man, two small girls, and an infant boy killed
summary: The 1887 posse (Game Warden Burgett, Sheriff Kendall) burned Colorow's camp, including property of Chipeta; militia under Maj. Leslie and the posse then attacked the camp at dawn near the reservation line. The Commissioner reported four Utes killed (one man, two small girls, an infant boy), not eight, and losses of over 600 horses and nearly 2,500 sheep and goats.

citation: ARCIA 1881, Report of the Ute Commission (Uncompahgre removal); 21 Stat. 199-200; ARCIA 1881, Report of the Ute Commission (to Manypenny), pp. ~325-329
quote: We examined the land on the Grand River near the mouth of the Gunnison, and found it to be, in our opinion, unsuit- able for the Indians for agricultural or grazing purposes.
summary: The 1880 agreement sent the Uncompahgre to Grand River near the Gunnison "if a sufficient quantity of agricultural land shall be found there", and otherwise to land "in that vicinity and in the Territory of Utah". The commissioners assigned to the Uncompahgre selection (the report names Mears and Russell building the new agency and McMorris paying improvement claims) reported the Grand River land unsuitable. That this report was knowingly false and motivated by Mears's interest is PSL's accusation, not established by the primary record.

citation: ICC Docket 349, Findings of Fact on the Stipulated Settlement (Feb. 18, 1965); ICC Docket 349, 14 Ind. Cl. Comm. 707, Findings 1, 4
quote: had no obligation to furnish such a reservation
summary: In Docket 349 the Uncompahgre claim was that the US never gave them a reservation in Colorado or Utah as the 1880 agreement required; the US denied any such obligation. The case ended in a compromise settlement, a net $300,000 judgment after offsets, entered Feb. 18, 1965. It is a settlement, not a finding that the US failed its obligation.

quote: With the massacre in mind, Congress decided to remove the Indians from the Colorado reservation as part of the punishment meted out for this tragedy.
summary: After the 1879 Meeker/Milk Creek fighting, Congress used the 1880 Act to punish the Utes and remove them from Colorado, barring payments until the participants surrendered and deducting victims' compensation from land proceeds. The Uncompahgre were removed too though they had no role in the incident.

citation: Ute treaty Mar. 2, 1868 Art. 2; Act of June 15, 1880; 15 Stat. 619, Art. 2; 21 Stat. 199, ch. 223
quote: fifteen miles due north of where said meridian
summary: Art. 2 reserved Colorado west of the 107th meridian and south of a line 15 miles north of the 40th parallel (566+616+617, about 16 million acres in repo polygons). Brunot (1873) took the San Juan strip (566); after the 1879 Meeker events the 1880 act removed White River and Uncompahgre Utes, leaving the Southern Ute strip (617).

quote: the claim in this case is res judicata under the 1950 consent judgment
summary: The ICC (1966) held the Southern Utes entitled to compensation for 230,547.44 acres disposed of under the 1895 Act and an accounting incl. 81,953.18 more acres; it found (1969) Royce 617 was never intended in the 1950 Confederated Ute settlement. The Supreme Court in 1971 held the claim res judicata under the 1950 consent judgment, ruling the 1880 Act ceded all non-allotted land; Docket 328 barred July 14, 1971.

quote: This relinquishment comprises that portion of the country assigned them by unratified Fort Laramie treaty of Sept. 17, 1851, not included within the
summary: Crow country recognized in 1851 (30.1 million acres in repo polygon 517) was relinquished outside an 1868 reservation, which was then cut in 1880-82 (619) and 1891 (714), leaving 715.

citation: Kappler II (1903 ed.); 11 Stat. 749 note; Kappler II 440-442 (1903 ed.), Art. 7; 11 Stat. 749
quote: This assent of all the Tribes has not been obtained
summary: The Senate amended Art. 7 to $50,000 a year for ten years, with up to five more at the President's discretion (Kappler prints the amended text). citation: Executive order of Nov. 26, 1884; Act of June 3, 1926; Kappler I (1904) 860; 44 Stat. 690, ch. 459, sec. 1
quote: set apart as a reserva tion for the use and occupation of the Northern Cheyenne Indians, now residing in the southern portion of Montana Territory
summary: The Northern Cheyenne had no reservation of their own from the 1868 treaty until the executive order of Nov. 26, 1884, about 16 years, not 20. Congress declared the reservation (as set by the 1900 order) tribal property only in 1926.

citation: Blackfoot treaty Oct. 17, 1855; Royce 1899 Schedule; 11 Stat. 657, Art. 3; Royce 1899 p. 855 (remarks)
quote: shall be a common hunting-ground for ninety-nine years
summary: Fort Laramie 1851 Art. 5 described a Blackfoot territory; whether any Blackfeet attended or signed was not checked (Kappler does not print the signatures). The 1855 treaty recognized Blackfoot territory and made a large tract a common hunting ground for 99 years. A treaty of Sept. 1, 1868 that would have reduced it was never ratified; per Royce the Executive order of July 5, 1873 (and later orders, the 1874 act and the 1888 agreement) cut it down.

citation: Montana Historical Society (IEFA lesson; Henderson, Montana Magazine 2018) via search; 18 Stat. 28 [unchecked]; 25 Stat. 113
summary: Baker's 2nd Cavalry attacked Heavy Runner's Piikani camp on Jan. 23, 1870, not the band sought; the Army's count was 173 dead, mostly women, children and elders, and Henderson gives 217. The 1873-74 reductions followed but no source here ties them to the massacre.

quote: permanent home to the whole Creek Nation of Indians
summary: The 1832 and 1833 treaties promised the Creeks a 'permanent home' with a fee patent (issued 1852). The 1866 treaty took the western half (486/698); allotment followed. McGirt held the 1866 reservation was never disestablished.
